'''Bart Andrew Kosko''' (born February 7, 1960) is an American writer and professor of electrical engineering and law at the [[University of Southern California]] (USC). He is a researcher and popularizer of [[fuzzy logic]], [[neural network]]s, and noise, and the author of several trade books and textbooks on these and related subjects of [[Artificial intelligence|machine intelligence]]. He was awarded the 2022 [[Donald O. Hebb]] Award for neural learning by the International Neural Network Society.<ref>{{Cite web|title=INNS Award Recipients|url=https://www.inns.org/inns-award-recipients|access-date=2023-07-27|website=www.inns.org}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|title=Kosko receives Hebb Award from International Neural Network Society|url=https://viterbischool.usc.edu/news/2023/06/kosko-receives-hebb-award-from-international-neural-network-society/|access-date=2023-07-27|website=www.usc.edu}}</ref>

==Personal background==
Kosko holds bachelor's degrees in philosophy and in economics from USC (1982), a master's degree in applied mathematics from UC San Diego (1983), a PhD in electrical engineering from UC Irvine (1987) under Allen Stubberud,<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Adam |first1=John A. |title=Bart Kosko: This optimistic engineer seeks to give machines a higher IQ—both in his neural and fuzzy systems work and in his prolific science fiction |journal=IEEE Spectrum |date=February 1996 |volume=33 |issue=2 |pages=58–62 |doi=10.1109/6.482276 |s2cid=1761292 }}</ref> and a J.D. from [[Concord Law School]]. He is an attorney licensed in [[California]] and federal court, and worked part-time as a [[law clerk]] for the [[Los Angeles County District Attorney|Los Angeles District Attorney]]'s Office.

Kosko is a political and religious [[Skepticism|skeptic]]. He is a contributing editor of the [[Libertarianism|libertarian]] periodical ''[[Liberty (1987)|Liberty]]'', where he has published essays on "Palestinian vouchers".<ref>{{cite web | url = http://www.libertyunbound.com/node/369 | title = Liberty Magazine – November 2003 }}</ref>

==Writing==
Kosko's most popular book to date was the international best-seller ''Fuzzy Thinking'', about man and machines thinking in shades of gray, and his most recent book was ''Noise''. He has also published [[Short story|short fiction]] and the cyber-thriller [[novel]] ''Nanotime'', about a [[World War III in popular culture|possible World War III]] that takes place in two days of the year 2030. The novel's title coins the term "nanotime" to describe the time speed-up that occurs when fast computer chips, rather than slow brains, house minds.

Kosko has a minimalist prose style, not even using commas in his book Noise.<ref>{{cite magazine| url=https://www.wired.com/2006/08/now-hear-this/| title=Now Hear This!| magazine=Wired}}</ref>

==Research==
Kosko's technical contributions have been in three main areas: [[fuzzy logic]], neural networks, and noise.

In fuzzy logic, he introduced [[fuzzy cognitive map]]s,<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Kosko|first=Bart|date= January 1986|title=Fuzzy cognitive maps|journal=International Journal of Man-Machine Studies|volume=24|issue=1|pages=65–75|doi=10.1016/S0020-7373(86)80040-2}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Julie|first1=Dickerson|last2=Kosko|first2=Bart|date= May 1994|title=Virtual Worlds as Fuzzy Cognitive Maps|journal= Presence: Teleoperators and Virtual Environments|volume=3|issue=2|pages=173–189|doi=10.1162/pres.1994.3.2.173|s2cid=61432716 }}</ref> fuzzy subsethood,<ref name=fuzzyEntropy>{{Cite journal|last=Kosko|first=Bart|date= December 1986|title=Fuzzy entropy and conditioning|journal=Information Sciences|volume=40|issue=2|pages=165–174|doi=10.1016/0020-0255(86)90006-X}}</ref> additive fuzzy systems,<ref name=globalStability>{{Cite journal|last=Kosko|first=Bart|date= August 1998|title=Global stability of generalized additive fuzzy systems|journal= IEEE Transactions on Systems, Man, and Cybernetics - Part C: Applications and Reviews|volume=28|issue=3|pages=441–452|doi=10.1109/5326.704584 |bibcode=1998ITHMS..28..441K }}</ref> fuzzy approximation theorems,<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Kosko|first=Bart|date=November 1994|title=Fuzzy systems as universal approximators|journal=IEEE Transactions on Computers|volume=43|issue=11|pages=1329–1333|doi=10.1109/12.324566 |bibcode=1994ITCmp..43.1329K }}</ref> optimal fuzzy rules,<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Kosko|first=Bart|date=1995|title=Optimal fuzzy rules cover extrema|journal=International Journal of Intelligent Systems|volume=10|issue=2|pages=249–255|doi=10.1002/int.4550100206|s2cid=205966636 }}</ref> fuzzy associative memories, various neural-based adaptive fuzzy systems,<ref name=globalStability/> ratio measures of fuzziness,<ref name=fuzzyEntropy/> the shape of fuzzy sets,<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Mitaim|first1=Sanya|last2=Kosko|first2=Bart|date=August 2001|title=The shape of fuzzy sets in adaptive function approximation|journal=IEEE Transactions on Fuzzy Systems|volume=9|issue=4|pages=249–255|doi=10.1109/91.940974 |bibcode=2001ITFS....9..637M }}</ref> the conditional variance of fuzzy systems,<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Lee|first1=Ian|last2=Kosko|first2=Bart|last3=Anderson|first3=W. French|date=November 2005|title=Modeling Gunshot Bruises in Soft Body Armor with an Adaptive Fuzzy System|journal= IEEE Transactions on Systems, Man, and Cybernetics - Part B: Cybernetics|volume=35|issue=6|pages=1374–1390|doi=10.1109/TSMCB.2005.855585|pmid=16366262 |bibcode=2005ITSMB..35.1374L |s2cid=1405236 }}</ref> and the geometric view of (finite) fuzzy sets as points in hypercubes and its relationship to the ongoing debate of fuzziness versus [[probability]].

In neural networks, Kosko introduced the unsupervised technique of differential [[Hebbian theory|Hebbian learning]],<ref name=UnsupervisedLearning>{{Cite journal|last=Kosko|first=Bart|date=March 1990|title=Unsupervised learning in noise|journal= IEEE Transactions on Neural Networks|volume=1|issue=1|pages=44–57|doi=10.1109/72.80204|pmid=18282822 |bibcode=1990ITNN....1...44K |s2cid=14223472 }}</ref> sometimes called the "differential synapse," and most famously the [[Bidirectional Associative Memory|BAM or bidirectional associative memory]]<ref name=BAM>{{Cite journal|last=Kosko|first=Bart|date=March 1988|title=Bidirectional associative memories|journal= IEEE Transactions on Systems, Man, and Cybernetics|volume=18|issue=1|pages=49–60|doi=10.1109/21.87054 |bibcode=1988ITSMC..18...49K }}</ref> family of feedback neural architectures, with corresponding global stability theorems.<ref name=UnsupervisedLearning/>

In [[colors of noise|noise]], Kosko introduced the concept of adaptive [[stochastic resonance]],<ref name=SR>{{Cite journal|last1=Mitaim|first1=Sanya|last2=Kosko|first2=Bart|date=November 1998|title=Adaptive stochastic resonance|journal= Proceedings of the IEEE|volume=86|issue=11|pages=2152–2183|doi=10.1109/5.726785 |bibcode=1998IEEEP..86.2152M }}</ref> using neural-like learning algorithms to find the optimal level of noise to add to many nonlinear systems to improve their performance. He proved many versions of the so-called "forbidden interval theorem," which guarantees that noise will benefit a system if the average level of noise does not fall in an interval of values.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Kosko|first1=Bart|last2=Mitaim|first2=Sanya|date=July 2003|title=Stochastic resonance in noisy threshold neurons|journal=Neural Networks|volume=16|issue=5–6|pages=755–761|doi=10.1016/S0893-6080(03)00128-X|pmid=12850031 }}</ref> He also showed that noise can speed up the convergence of Markov chains to equilibrium.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Brandon|first1=Franzke|last2=Kosko|first2=Bart|date=October 2011|title=Noise can speed convergence in Markov chains|journal= Physical Review E|volume=84 |issue=4 |article-number=041112 |doi=10.1103/PhysRevE.84.041112|pmid=22181092 |bibcode=2011PhRvE..84d1112F }}</ref>
